# Moving Data Around {#chp:data}

Sooner or later you need to hand data to something that is not R: a web page,
a JavaScript library, a config file, or an HTML file that must carry its own
attachments. This chapter covers the encodings that make that easy: base64, JSON,
and YAML.

## Base64 {#sec:base64}

Base64 turns any bytes into plain text, which is how a file can travel inside an
HTML page or a JSON string.

### Encode and decode bytes {#sec:base64-bytes}

`base64_encode()` and `base64_decode()` convert between raw bytes and base64
strings:

```{r}
raw_bytes = charToRaw("Hello, xfun!")
(b64 = base64_encode(raw_bytes))
rawToChar(base64_decode(b64))
```

### Embed a file as a data URI {#sec:base64-uri}

`base64_uri()` goes one step further and makes a data URI, which embeds a file
directly in HTML. It is the mechanism behind `xfun::embed_file()`. Here are the
first characters of one:

```{r}
f = system.file("LICENSE", package = "xfun")
substr(base64_uri(f), 1, 60)
```

## JSON {#sec:json}

`tojson()` is a small JSON serializer with no dependencies. It was written to
send data from R to JavaScript, so it has a few extras: it can emit JavaScript
instead of strict JSON, and it can shrink long vectors. The examples below use
`cat()` so you see the text exactly as a browser would receive it.

### Turn R objects into JSON {#sec:tojson}

Named lists become objects, unnamed lists become arrays, matrices go by row, and
data frames go by column:

```{r, comment='', attr.output='.js'}
cat(tojson(list(x = 1:3, y = c(TRUE, FALSE), z = NULL)))
cat(tojson(head(iris, 3)))   # data frame: columns
cat(tojson(matrix(1:6, 2)))  # matrix: rows
```

### Embed JavaScript in the JSON {#sec:js}

Need a callback in your configuration? Wrap a string in `js()` and it is written
as raw JavaScript, with no quotes:

```{r, comment='', attr.output='.js'}
cat(tojson(list(n = 42, callback = js("function(x) { return x * 2; }"))))
```

That is not valid JSON anymore, but it is valid JavaScript, which is often all
you need.

### Choose between JavaScript and strict JSON {#sec:json-mode}

By default (`mode = "js"`) the output is JavaScript, which can hold things that
JSON cannot. Compare the same object in both modes. In JavaScript mode, a
date-time becomes `new Date(...)` and infinity stays `Infinity`:

```{r, comment='', attr.output='.js'}
x = list(
  day = as.Date("2026-11-08"),
  time = as.POSIXct("2026-11-08 09:30:00", tz = "UTC"),
  values = c(1, Inf, -Inf, NA)
)
cat(tojson(x))
```

For output that `JSON.parse()` accepts, use `mode = "json"`. The date-time
becomes an ISO 8601 string, and `Inf` becomes `null`, just like `NA`:

```{r, comment='', attr.output='.json'}
cat(tojson(x, mode = "json"))
```

### Shrink repeated values {#sec:dict}

When a vector repeats the same few values many times, writing every copy is
wasteful. With `dict = 1`, `tojson()` stores the unique values once and the
vector as indices into them. In JavaScript mode it rebuilds the strings right in
the output with `.map()`:

```{r, comment='', attr.output='.js'}
x = rep(c("apple", "banana", "cherry"), 4)
cat(tojson(x, pretty = FALSE))
cat(tojson(x, dict = 1, pretty = FALSE))
```

In strict JSON mode, the two parts are stored as an object, with the unique values
under one key and the indices under another (the keys start with an invisible
control character, so they never clash with your own names):

```{r, comment='', attr.output='.json'}
cat(tojson(x, dict = 1, mode = "json", pretty = FALSE))
```

On a longer vector the saving is real. Here are 300 values:

```{r}
x = rep(c("apple", "banana", "cherry"), 100)
nchar(tojson(x, pretty = FALSE))            # without dict encoding
nchar(tojson(x, dict = 1, pretty = FALSE))  # with dict encoding
```

The number you give `dict` is a threshold on the share of unique values: a
vector is encoded when its unique values are at most `dict` times its length.
Here 3 of 12 values are unique (0.25), so `dict = 0.5` encodes it and
`dict = 0.2` leaves it alone. `tojson()` also skips the encoding whenever it
would not make the output shorter, which is why short or nearly unique vectors
come out unchanged.

### Ship big integer vectors compactly {#sec:json-pack}

Long integer vectors can be packed as base64 with `tojson(pack = n)`, where `n`
is the minimum length to pack. The array of numbers becomes one short string.
Here is the start of each version of a vector of 1 to 200:

```{r, comment='', attr.output='.json'}
x = list(a = 1:200)
cat(substr(tojson(x, pretty = FALSE), 1, 60), "...")
cat(substr(tojson(x, pack = 10, mode = "json", pretty = FALSE), 1, 60), "...")
```

Mind the byte counts:

```{r}
nchar(tojson(x, pretty = FALSE))
nchar(tojson(x, pack = 10, mode = "json", pretty = FALSE))
```

The packed object has a key that names the type of the typed array (`u8` for
unsigned 8-bit integers here), and the base64 string holds the bytes. In the
default JavaScript mode, the same vector appears as an `unpack({...})` call.

The browser needs to turn the base64 string back into a typed array. That is
what `json_unpack` and `json_reviver` are for. Both are plain character strings
of JavaScript, ready to paste into a `<script>`.

### Unpack packed values in the browser {#sec:json-unpack}

`json_unpack` defines a JavaScript function `unpack(o)` that decodes one packed
object (a plain array is returned as is) on demand. Use it when you parse the JSON yourself and want to unpack only the
fields you need:

```{r, comment='', attr.output='.js'}
cat(json_unpack)
```

### Revive packed values while parsing {#sec:json-reviver}

`json_reviver` includes `unpack()` and also defines `reviver`, so
`JSON.parse(text, reviver)` expands packed and dictionary-encoded values
automatically as it parses. Prefer `unpack()` for large payloads, since a reviver
runs on every parsed value. Here is the part that `json_reviver` adds on top of
`json_unpack`:

```{r, comment='', attr.output='.js'}
cat(substr(json_reviver, nchar(json_unpack) + 2, nchar(json_reviver)))
```

### Convert a single vector to JSON {#sec:json-vector}

`tojson()` handles whole objects. For one atomic vector, `json_vector()` is the
building block underneath. It returns the elements as strings (quoted by
default, `NA` becomes `null`), or a single array string with `to_array = TRUE`:

```{r}
json_vector(c("a", "b", NA))
json_vector(c("a", "b", NA), to_array = TRUE)
json_vector(c(1, NA, Inf), to_array = TRUE, quote = FALSE)
```

## YAML and TAML {#sec:yaml}

YAML is the usual choice for configuration and document metadata. The **yaml**
package parses all of it, but it is a dependency. TAML ("tiny YAML") is the small
subset that covers most config files, parsed with no packages at all.

### Read simple YAML without dependencies {#sec:taml-load}

`taml_load()` parses TAML, a tiny subset of YAML (scalars, one-level nesting,
and inline arrays like `[1, 2]`), with no need for the **yaml** package.
R code tagged with `!expr` is evaluated unless you pass `envir = FALSE`:

```{r}
x = c("a: 1", "b: [1, 2]", "c: !expr 1 + 1", "d:", "  e: true")
str(taml_load(x))
str(taml_load(x, envir = FALSE))
```

### Read TAML from a file {#sec:taml-file}

`taml_file()` is `taml_load()` for a path:

```{r}
f = tempfile(fileext = ".yml")
writeLines(c("title: Hello", "tags: [\"a\", \"b\"]"), f)
str(taml_file(f))
```

### Write a list as TAML {#sec:taml-save}

`taml_save()` is the inverse. It returns the lines, or writes them to a file
when you give `path`:

```{r}
cfg = list(title = "Hi", n = 2, tags = c("a", "b"), sub = list(ok = TRUE))
taml_save(cfg)
f = tempfile(fileext = ".yml")
taml_save(cfg, f)
str(taml_file(f))
```

### Parse YAML with whatever is available {#sec:yaml-load}

`yaml_load()` uses the **yaml** package when it is installed and falls back to
`taml_load()` otherwise. Force the fallback with `use_yaml = FALSE`:

```{r}
yaml_load("a: 1\nb: [x, y]", use_yaml = FALSE)
```

### Split YAML metadata from the body {#sec:yaml-body}

`yaml_body()` splits a document into its front matter and the rest. The result
has the parsed `yaml`, its `lines` range, and the `body`, in which the YAML
lines are blanked so line numbers stay put. Use `parse = FALSE` to get the raw
YAML text:

```{r}
doc = c("---", "title: Hello", "---", "", "Content.")
str(yaml_body(doc))
yaml_body(doc, parse = FALSE)$yaml
```
